text: Winifred Emms (4 April 1883 – 28 September 1972), best known by her stage name Hetty King, was an English entertainer who performed in music halls as a male impersonator for approximately 70 years. Born in New Brighton, Cheshire, she was raised in an itinerant family usually based in Manchester; her father, William Emms (1856–1954), was a comedian and musician who performed as Billy King and managed Uncle Billy's Minstrels, a travelling troupe that used portable theatres and caravans. As a child, she began appearing in her father's shows, imitating popular performers of the day, and adopted the name Hetty King when she first performed at the Shoreditch Theatre at the age of six. At ten, she won a contest that provided her with a season’s work at Blackpool Pier. She began performing as a solo act in music halls around 1902, though she appeared as a vocalist and dancer at the Argyle Theatre Birkenhead as early as December 1898. In her early career, she developed a precise impression of the lion comique George Lashwood. For the week beginning 10 December 1904, she topped the programme at the newly opened Empire Theatre in Ashton-under-Lyne, billed as "The Society Gem," marking her first of many appearances there as part of W. H. Broadhead's theatre circuit. She began performing regularly as a male impersonator in 1905, starring in Dick Whittington at the Kennington Theatre, thereafter appearing regularly dressed as a "swell." In 1907, she travelled to the United States with Canadian comedian R. G. Knowles, setting records at the New York Theatre and performing songs such as "I Want a Gibson Girl" and "When I Get Back To Piccadilly." After returning to England, she began performing "Ship Ahoy! (All the Nice Girls Love a Sailor)," written by Bennett Scott and A. J. Mills, which she first sang at the Liverpool Empire in 1908 but only became successful in 1909, when it was described as the greatest pantomime hit for four years and became her signature song. Her career spanned both World Wars, during which she performed in the uniform of either a soldier or a sailor; in the First World War, she toured in France and Belgium, entertaining troops. In 1915, she performed with her husband Ernest Lotinga at a fundraiser for The Evening News Prisoners of War Fund at the Prince of Wales Hotel in Hampton Court, which included around 30 wounded soldiers, and all artists performed for free. In 1916, her act included "Songs the Soldiers Sing," featuring songs composed by soldiers in the trenches. By around 1930, she was reputedly the highest-paid music hall star in the world, largely due to her meticulous study of the mannerisms of men such as sailors and soldiers, including how to march, salute, light a pipe, and swing a kitbag correctly, while ensuring her femininity remained evident—sometimes winking at the audience to reveal the subterfuge. She also played the "principal boy" in many pantomimes and appeared on BBC Radio, being described in 1933 as the "most virile of male impersonators" and a long-standing broadcasting favourite. She continued performing until her death, regularly touring in the United States, Australia, and South Africa, and by the late 1930s was regarded as a nostalgia act. From 1948, she toured Britain as one of the veteran performers in Don Ross’s show Thanks for the Memory. She was known for insisting on top billing and was described as "stubborn, uncompromising and a legend in the business for cantankerous and temperamental behaviour, refusing to consider any other type of performance as fashions changed." In 1901, she married actor and writer Ernie Lotinga (1876–1951), born in Sunderland; he was a music hall comedian, singer, and theatre proprietor, billed as Dan Roe from 1898, and appeared in films in the 1920s and 1930s as PC Jimmy Josser. They had one child and divorced in 1917, with a decree nisi granted on 16 March by Sir Samuel Evans on grounds of King's misconduct with vaudeville artist and actor Jack Norworth, a divorce not contested. Her second marriage, in 1918, was to Alexander Lamond. Her half-sister, Olive Emms, was also an actress who often travelled with her and served as her dresser; her half-brother, Harold Emms, co-wrote many of King’s songs with his French wife, Francine. King died in Wimbledon, London, in 1972 at the age of 89 and was cremated at Golders Green Crematorium. On 8 November 2010, a commemorative blue plaque was installed at her last residence in Wimbledon by the theatre charity The Music Hall Guild of Great Britain and America. Hetty King appeared in the film Lilacs in the Spring (1954), directed by Herbert Wilcox and starring Anna Neagle and Errol Flynn, and in a film titled Hetty King – Performer (1970) at the end of her career, aged 87.
